big: Two multi-asset funds can wear the same label and carry very different risks. The difference is written in the factsheet, in a few lines. Learn which lines to read before you pitch.

lines: Both funds say 65% equity in their one-page summary. Aren't they the same, then?
Not yet. One line is gross equity. Another shows what is hedged. Let us open both factsheets side by side.

alt: Two bars with the same 65 percent gross equity: one fully exposed, one with 30 percent hedged arbitrage
caps: Fund P and Fund Q both show gross equity of 65%. Gross counts arbitrage positions too.
In Fund P, all 65% is real market exposure. Net equity: 65%.
In Fund Q, 30% is hedged arbitrage: a stock bought, the same stock sold in futures. Net equity: 35%.
Net equity is what moves with the market. Same gross, nearly half the exposure.

alt: Two bars comparing yield to maturity, duration, and price dip if yields rise by half a point
caps: For the debt sleeve read two numbers. YTM: the yield the bonds offer if held to maturity.
Modified duration: how sensitive the price is to interest rates, in years.
If yields rise 0.5 point, the price dips about duration times 0.5: about 2% at four years, 0.5% at one.
The longer sleeve offers 0.6 point more yield, and takes four times the dip.

intro: A made-up factsheet for a multi-asset fund. What each line tells you.
note: Gross 65% plus debt 20% plus gold and silver 15% make 100%. Net equity is gross minus the hedged part. Funds differ widely in their commodity weights, so compare them.

q: Fund P and Fund Q both show gross equity of 65%. Q has 30% in hedged arbitrage. Equity markets fall 20%. Roughly how much does the equity part cost each fund's NAV?
opts: About 13 points for both, since both funds show the same gross equity figure
About 13 points for P and 7 points for Q, because net equity is 65% and 35%
About 7 points for both, since the hedge protects every fund's equity part
About 7 points for P and 13 points for Q, since arbitrage makes a fund riskier
why: Gross includes hedged positions, so it overstates Q's exposure to a market fall. Net equity decides.
Hedged arbitrage does not move with the market. P's 65% times 20% is 13; Q's 35% times 20% is 7.
Only Q holds the hedge. P has no arbitrage to offset anything, so it takes the full 13 points.
Arbitrage is hedged. It adds little market risk, which is why Q's exposure is lower, not higher.

q: A client wants about a third of her fund exposed to the equity market. Which factsheet line shows that?
opts: Gross equity, because it adds up everything the fund holds in equity shares
YTM, because it measures how much of the fund is invested in the market
Fund size, because a large fund holds more equity than a smaller one does
Net equity, since it removes hedged arbitrage and shows real exposure
why: Gross includes hedged positions. A fund with a 65% gross may carry far less market exposure.
YTM describes the yield of the debt sleeve. It says nothing about the share held in equity.
Size says how much money the fund holds, not how it splits between equity and other assets.
Net equity is gross minus the hedged arbitrage, so it is what actually moves with the market.

q: Sleeve B has YTM 7.6% and modified duration 4.0 years. Sleeve A has 7.0% and 1.0 years. Yields rise 0.5 point. About how much does B's price fall?
opts: About 2.0%, since duration of 4.0 times a 0.5 point rise gives 2.0
About 0.5%, since that is the size of the rise in yields themselves
About 0.125%, since 0.5 is divided by the duration of 4.0 years
About 8%, since 4.0 years divided by 0.5 gives the percentage fall
why: Price change is roughly duration times the yield change: 4.0 times 0.5 is 2.0%. A's fall is about 0.5%.
0.5% is the dip for A, with one year of duration. B's longer duration multiplies the move four times.
Dividing by duration reverses the logic. Longer duration makes the price move more, not less.
Dividing 4.0 by 0.5 gives 8, but duration multiplies the yield change. The right figure is 2.0%.

q: Fund X holds gold 12% and silver 3%. Fund Y holds gold 25% and silver 10%. A client says all multi-asset funds hold about the same commodities. What is the fair reply?
opts: Yes, since SEBI fixes the same commodity weights for every multi-asset fund
Yes, because only gold counts and every fund holds roughly the same amount
No. Weights differ widely, 15% in X and 35% in Y, so their rides will differ
No, because Y holds silver and silver always rises when gold falls in the market
why: SEBI sets a 10% minimum per asset class, not a fixed commodity weight. Funds choose their own.
Silver and gold are both commodity engines. Their weights differ widely, so it matters how much of each.
X has 15% in gold and silver, Y has 35%. Y leans far more on commodities, so it responds to them far more.
Silver has no rule of rising when gold falls. Calling it a fixed pattern would repeat the same error.

pts: Read gross and net equity: net removes hedged arbitrage and shows the real market exposure.
For the debt sleeve read YTM (the yield) and modified duration (the rate sensitivity). A price dip is about duration times the rise in yields.
Commodity weights range widely between funds. Open the factsheet before you pitch.
